utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just two points before we continue with the examination-in-chief. First, it is absolutely essential that the evidence of this witness be completed today, and the Chamber expects full cooperation from all parties in that regard. Secondly, Mr. Greaves, the registrar, with her customary efficiency has investigated the matter you brought to our attention and it can be easily put down to a miscommunication and misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Mundis: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you were describing the geographic layout of your village in relation to the town of Prijedor. I would ask the usher show a copy of the map that has been distributed to the witness. If we can briefly do that, please. Witness, can you see the map that's been placed on the ELMO to your left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you -- you recognise your village on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Donja Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, does this map accurately reflect the various villages and towns that are depicted on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so, really. It looks as if from Prijedor towards Rakovcani which is -- which I don't think is correct, because it is likely more to the left, not exactly in that direction. Hambarine is okay, Donja Ljubija, and Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness. If the usher could retrieve the copy of that map, please. Yesterday when we completed your testimony, we were about to move into the conditions in Room 4. Can you please describe for the Court the conditions in Room 4 when you first were placed in that room, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room which was overcrowded, people sat on pallets, wooden pallets, some sat on the floor. To the right of the door there was a small toilet and people were there too. It was terribly dirty because the air was stale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many people were in Room 4 when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's move on to the general conditions in Keraterm while you were there. Can you please describe for the Court the sanitary conditions as well as the food and access to water, those type of conditions in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. Calls for a narrative answer, compounded question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "Can you describe the sanitary conditions as well as the food and access?" You are saying he has asked several questions? He's asking generally about the sanitary condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I was only objecting to the form of the question, because it's a compounded question and invites the witness to give a narration. That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just simplify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the sanitary conditions in Keraterm, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. The sewage was blocked. To reach the toilet you have to wade there through the water of some ten centimetres deep, with excrement flowing in it. When we went to eat, we always had the same dishes with the same spoons, and vessels from which we ate our food. There was already old, stale food. We rarely had an opportunity to wash those vessels. In front of the room there was a barrel for water but -- when there was water in it, we could wash ourselves, but there was seldom water in it. To the toilet, we could go, depending on the situation in the camp itself. At times we could go freely. At times they sent us in an organised manner. And at times we could not go there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there facilities available to wash your clothing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe for the court the conditions with respect to meal times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had one meal a day, if there was food for everybody, and if we were allowed to go to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of food were you served on those occasions when you were allowed to eat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could hardly call it food. It was water with a leaf or two, or perhaps pasta, a slice of bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, shortly after your arrival at Keraterm, did you become aware of the camp structure with respect to personnel in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there guards in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, yes. Do you mean the ethnic structure?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the organisational structure of the camp personnel. Were the guards structured in any way to your knowledge during the time that you were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some were in military and some in police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they organised into any kinds of shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how the shifts were organised, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did there appear to be any type of command structure within the shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every shift had its commander, and that includes the camp. The camp also had a commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many shifts there were at the time that you were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know exactly. I know only some of the shifts and what I heard from others, but I'd rather not talk about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of who the shift commanders were at Keraterm during the time that you were present there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: So for Damir Dosenovic, called Kajin, I'm sure, and as for the others, only what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person that you've referred to as Kajin, did you know him prior to the time that you were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For approximately how long did you know him prior to your arrival at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about eight, nine years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of those eight or nine years, approximately how many times had you seen this person that you describe as Kajin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very often, a few times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come to know this person that you knew as Kajin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drasko, his brother, was my school pal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you think that you could identify the person that you knew as Kajin if you were to see him today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would ask you to take a look around the courtroom, and if the person that you know as Kajin is present, if you could please indicate that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, please, with respect to the row that he's sitting in and his place in that row?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the back row, in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not counting the police, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, counting the positions from left to right in the back row, can you please tell us which seat he's sitting in, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second from left to right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what he's wearing, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: A suit, a white shirt, and a dotted tie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you were counting the position that he was in, were you including or excluding the police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excluding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the record reflect that the witness has properly identified the accused, Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during the time that you were in Keraterm, did you see this person that you have identified as Kajin in the camp, and if so, how frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, while you were in the Keraterm camp, did you witness any mistreatment of the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I also participated in one of them. That is, I was also mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's begin with the mistreatment of other detainees, not yourself. Can you please describe for the court what you witnessed while Blank page inserted to insure pagination corresponds between the French and the English transcripts you were in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about some of the things that I saw, and there were other things about which I only heard. As for the things that I saw, I was mistreated myself. And I can talk about things that I heard. And I can do that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's start with that. Can you describe incidents that you say that you've heard, starting with the first day or two that you were in Keraterm camp, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very day that I was brought in, but towards the evening, another group from Ljubija was brought in. Of them, and I won't give his name, I'll only give you his first name, and that is Hasan, was taken out and brought right in front of our -- of Room 4, that is our room, and somebody began to beat him. I could not see who that was, and I cannot say exactly how long it took, but the screams were horrible and he survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how long you heard these screams?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ten minutes, could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during the first couple of days that you were in Keraterm, did you hear or do you recall hearing any gunfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nonstop. At all hours of day or night one could hear gunshots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if those gunshots were coming from within the camp or from the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person named Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Zoran Zigic in the Keraterm camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the ethnicity of the people that were being detained with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats, and a Serb here and there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were also Albanians detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite a number of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, in the first couple of days that you were in Keraterm, are you aware of any Albanians being called out of the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what you witnessed with respect to Albanians being called out, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days of my stay in Keraterm, a young man was called out who had come to the camp together with me. They took him out, started to beat him, and asked him, "Where's that tall one who had come with you?" And he said that that one was in Room 3. And they then responded by requesting that all Albanians in all rooms come out. And from the room that I was in, another Albanian who had arrived with me came forward, and a young man called Besim Jusufi came out, and then they began to beat all of them. After some time, they brought them back to the room. They were all bloody, had huge bloody bruises on the faces, on the body, black and blue bruises. They were in terrible pain, and they returned to the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them after they returned to the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fejzo, Besim Jusufi recovered quickly, and a third Albanian died after two or three days. He died on the third day. We carried him out of the room to the left of Room 4 and laid him down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you testified earlier that there were a couple of Serbs also in the camp. Do you recall any of the names of the Serbs who were in the Keraterm camp with you as detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Jovo Radocaj. The second day after I got to the camp at night-time, a Serb was brought, he was brought by a Serb from his own locality, a Serb policeman. And at the -- in the reception office of the camp he was met by Damir slapped him in the face and asked him, "What dick made you? What Serb are you? What Serb dick could make you?" And he was then ordered to go into one of the rooms and told that he'd get his desserts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the gentleman has used universally known word for male sexual organ, penis, and here in translation it's something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we take note of that. Continue, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you say he was met by Damir, who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kajin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the camp, did you see Jovo Radocaj at any other time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovo came to my room. It was twilight by that time, and as soon as it got darker, we could hear a group approaching the room in which we were detained. When I came near the door, we could hear the words, "Come on Serb, come out." Jovo stood up and went out and they began to beat him. I can't remember how long. All I do remember is the last blow after which silence ensued, and that blow sounded like when a wet ball hits the wall. And then the door opened again and Jovo was thrown at my feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know which shift was on duty at the time of this beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same shift as when Jovo was brought in, the shift which was commanded by Damir Dosenovic, called Kajin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know where Kajin was when this beating occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the group came to the room, I could not see them. The voice which called Jovo to come out sounded familiar. The man who was calling out Jovo to come out was Kajin's voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Jovo Radocaj was thrown back into the room, as you characterised it, did you see his condition upon his return to Room 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovo had coveralls buttoned up to the neck. His head was all bloody. He took a few hours to die. And he was rambling, trying to say something. I did understand some of it. He was calling out for his wife Zdenka, for his brothers, and spoke to goats - his wife and he were quite known for that - and things like that. And he died a few hours later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you the following day see anything that -- any physical markings on the building from the events that had happened the day before or the night before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a bloody stain on the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what that stain looked like, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Witness, you told the court that you knew Drago Tokmadzic. Did you see Drago Tokmadzic at any time in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you saw him, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No sooner did I arrive in the camp -- or rather after the first room, I was told that Eso and Drago were in Room 4, and that is where I went. There they made some room for me, and I stayed there in the same room with them all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Drago Tokmadzic called out of the room during the time that you were in Room 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One evening, a person came and went from room to room looking for Drago Tokmadzic. Drago was already getting ready or rather putting all the clothes he could on, and when that person reached Room 4, Drago responded, and that one told him to wait a little. And after a short time, one could hear that largish group was coming and Drago was ordered to come out -- or rather they first unlocked the door to the room and said that Drago should come out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Drago Tokmadzic actually go out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear or see what happened to him once he went out of the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. When he came out of the room, Drago said, "Come on, lads. My mother is a Serb too." And they -- whereupon they started to beat him, to swear at him. Somebody said, "You will beat Serb children, will you?" And then the question ensued, "Who came with you?" And he said, "Esad Islamovic." They were stopping to beat Drago, they also said, "Let's have Esad out." Esad came out, and he told them, "This is some mix-up because I am a Serb policeman. I've only come to make a statement." Whereupon they laughed and went on beating. And after a short while Drago and Eso could not be heard again. All we could hear is that somebody ordered "another hundred times" and one could hear blows as if with a wet cloth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you testified that Esad said he was a Serb policeman; was that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Esad a Serb policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the five of us were kicked out, the rest of those who remained had to sign an oath of loyalty to the Serbs, and those who did not wish to do so had -- actually, they were afraid, if they did not sign it, that later on, they would be kicked out one by one or taken to the camp like Drago and Eso. Drago and Eso were both disarmed after their shift and taken to the Keraterm camp still wearing their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity was Eso Islamovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, after Drago Tokmadzic and Esad Islamovic were taken out and beaten, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers who were standing next to the door ordered four men Blank page inserted to insure pagination corresponds between the French and the English transcripts out to carry them in. I stood up first. At the very door, this soldier hit me with a police baton over my head. I fell. And then from all sides they started kicking me and beating me with batons and with whatever else they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you recognise any of the people who were beating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how long did this beating take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a long time, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which shift was on duty when you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Damir Dosenovic's shift. His nickname is Kajin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the night before I entered the room and before the room was locked, the guards who were there and Kajin himself were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were being beaten, did you see Kajin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. My apologies. This is a leading question. He was asked whom he saw and he stated whom he saw. This is leading, this next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question is: "During the time that you were being beaten, did you see Kajin?" I see nothing leading in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies, the witness did answer that what -- that while he was being beaten, he did not see anyone. In other words, he said that he did not see who he was being beaten by. Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it is open to counsel to put a question specifically in relation to a particular person. Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were being beaten, did you see Kajin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw that they would not stop beating me and that I could not withstand all the beating, and expecting to be called out, I was considering what to do, just as everybody else did. I tried to defend by yelling out, "Pilip, Kajin, they are killing me," and this worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "this worked"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stopped beating me. One among them, "Listen to this," and the other one said, "Who is this one calling?" And from the group who were -- who had surrounded Drago and Eso, one person came over and he said, "Guys, stop." And this person was Damir Dosenovic, called Kajin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened, Witness, after you were beaten, can you please describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another three men came out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said, "Enough, let's go." "Enough, let's go." And the record says, "Enough, stop." This was in answer to the previous question of my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you are saying the answer was enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "Enough, we are going." Something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe what happened after you were beaten, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another three men came out of the room. We carried in Eso and then Drago and the door closed behind us and was locked. I passed a piece of cloth to Eso and Drago was asking for water. I gave him a drink, and he died. Shortly thereafter, I started losing consciousness, and somebody dragged me somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, prior to losing consciousness, can you -- did you see the condition that Drago Tokmadzic was in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were covered in blood. Drago was stripped to the waist. They were black and blue and virtually disfigured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you receive any type of injuries as a result of the beating and, if so, can you please describe them for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received many blows around the head. My nose was broken. I am not going to belabour the swellings. I was black and blue all over my body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us the condition that Eso Islamovic was in following the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to and raised my head, Eso's head looked like a bloody blot. You couldn't see the ears. You couldn't see the eyes. He was all swollen. His fingers were broken. It looked horrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Eso Islamovic after that, after you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several days later a doctor arrived, and we could hear them saying that if there were any sick people, that they should report to go to the hospital. And as Eso was not quite together, I asked him a couple of questions to see whether his mind was clear. I told him to say that he had fallen from a vehicle, which is what he did, and he was taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him after that and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see him. One evening when two vehicles came from Keraterm to Omarska, one friend pointed that Eso was under -- was under -- behind the window, but I could not see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after Eso was taken out of Keraterm, did you ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the date that you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19 June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that you left Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I neglected to ask you a couple of questions earlier. Let me ask those before I move on to the next area. When you first arrived at Keraterm on the 19th of June, how long after that time did you first get something to eat in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one last follow-up question with respect to eating times. Approximately how long, on those occasions when you were given food in Keraterm, how long were you allowed to eat the food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen if you didn't eat the food in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in those couple of minutes, it would sometimes happen that we would often be beaten, and the person who took lead in this was Banovic. We had to eat quickly, and even faster move back to the room where we were staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on the 4th of July, can you please tell us where you went when you left Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that we would be going to the camp at Ljubija and that all those who were from Ljubija should give their names to be put down on a list, and that buses would come to transfer us there. When we did all this, the buses arrived, we boarded them, and the buses took us to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything about how this list was utilised in the camp that you are talking about? You said a list, can you tell us anything about the list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kajin came and said to someone of the men from Ljubija that we should compile a list and that we would be going to Ljubija. And this is what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, go to Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, we went to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were with you on the bus that you travelled to Omarska in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two buses, but I wouldn't be able to give you the exact number. In addition to those of us who were from Ljubija, some others also boarded the buses after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the physical conditions of the people that were Blank page inserted to insure pagination corresponds between the French and the English transcripts on the bus that you travelled in, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended. Some who had been brought to Keraterm in the days prior to this were still in a good physical shape. Those of us who had come earlier or some who had come even before I had come were unshaven, filthy, and many of them were covered in blood like me with their clothes torn and beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how long did it take for the bus to travel from Keraterm to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: About one hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us what you saw when you arrived at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, that is when we first arrived, we had to keep our heads bowed. We were ordered to get off the buses. I could see the men on the pista and there were -- looked in terrible shape, but I only looked surreptitiously. Then they lined us against the wall. We had to raise our hands and keep three fingers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to restate my objection that I proposed yesterday, because early on there was a ruling in this Trial Chamber that these are going to be separate trials, Keraterm and Omarska. In the pre-trial conference that we had with the Prosecutor about a month, month and a half ago, it was suggested by Mr. Ryneveld that the evidence to be presented about Omarska will not be -- will be presented only as far as the genocide accounts, but not any other less accounts. I would just like to state it for the record and to have you be apprised of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. It's not only the genocide count to which the happenings at Omarska are relevant. They are the persecution counts which relate to the Prijedor area generally, and illustrative of that is what happened at Keraterm. Keraterm is identified specifically. But more generally, the persecution charges relate to the Prijedor area, in which Omarska would fall. So it seems to us that evidence of Omarska is very relevant. Mr. Mundis, do you have anything to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That summarises the position of the Prosecutor as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do appreciate what you have said, but as far as the persecution count -- part of the counts of the crimes against humanity, it would be very proper and fair to adduce the evidence as to at least what my client is charged with, evidence that he could see and could perceive at that time, because, as the witnesses have also testified, the Omarska is 25 kilometres away, and what had happened in opstina Prijedor that somebody in his position couldn't perceive would be very prejudicial. The only evidence that he could perceive at that time would be something that could be imputed to him, and whether he had observed it or not, that is going to be subject to another -- to the many, many other witnesses. But basically, establishing that charge should be based on what he could have perceived at that time, and unless this witness or other witness have seen him in Omarska, what happened in Omarska shouldn't be relevant to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. The Chamber is well aware of the proper basis for attributing criminal liability. The Chamber determines that evidence as to what took place at Omarska is very relevant to the indictment. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please describe for us anything that happened on the first night that you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the group that arrived in Omarska was recorded, we went to the garage, which was to the right of where the buses had come to a stop and where we got off. After a while they took us to another room where -- that previously were used as the mining company offices. After it grew dark, different groups started arriving. They were asking for money, for clothes, for shoes. They would bring some out, bring them back, beaten up, bloodied and bruised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when you were in Omarska that you personally were called out of the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court about that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: They selected three of us haphazardly and said that we would be taken to the "white house." They took us across the way to a room, and one of the three of us said that he knew Krkan and that they were close, and then I also said that I knew him. The two of us were then taken back with only -- having received only several blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe eating conditions or access to food in the Omarska camp, particularly with respect to the first few days that you were there, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they would take us to eat, we had to clear a number of obstacles, like chains that were stretched out, then some pipes, and we were hosed with water, and we were in a gauntlet of guards who beat us. We had to run and then get the food. Those who had sit down -- who had sat down first had to get up to make room for the new ones who were arriving. And then on the way back, we had to clear the same obstacles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you first given food after you arrived at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: After two or three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of food --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Further presentation of this evidence is going to cause impossibility, at least to this counsel, to effectively cross-examine this witness, because this was not anticipated. And your ruling of this Trial Chamber, as a matter of fact, has given full indicia that those are going to be two separate trials. The very fact that this statements -- statement that was presented beforehand did have some information about Keraterm, but that was a statement of a witness who could tell his experiences. However, it is a discretion of the Prosecutor to say what he is going to -- what testimony he is going to bring. And at the Pre-Trial Conference, we were deceived. We are not in a position to continue this effective representation on the issue of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's quite clear that the evidence is very Blank page inserted to insure pagination corresponds between the French and the English transcripts relevant, and the Chamber has ruled on this, but in the interests of clarification, I'm going to ask Mr. Mundis to comment on the statement made by counsel about the Pre-Trial Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Prosecutor's position that first of all, all three of the accused were put on notice with respect to the breadth of the Prosecutor's case by the 13 October, 2000, pre-trial brief in which extensive discussion was made as to the number of camps in Prijedor and the interlocking nature of those camps. Moreover, our 65 ter witness statements that were also filed in October of 2000 indicated witnesses would be testifying as to Omarska and Trnopolje and Manjaca as well. It's also our view that in Mr. Ryneveld's opening statement this has been raised, as well in the court witness summaries that have been provided on an ongoing basis to all three of the accused. With respect to the representations with respect to the Pre-Trial Conference, certainly representations were made that -- particularly the accused Kolundzija and Dosen, there is no evidence that they were ever in the Omarska camp. However, it is still our view that with respect to the -- particularly the genocide and as well as the persecution counts, that these matters are relevant. And certainly all three of the accused have been on notice that the Prosecutor was intending on leading this type of evidence, since at least October of 2000. And up until the moment Mr. Vucicevic raised in objection yesterday, that was the very first time that the Prosecutor was aware that any of the accused would be objecting to this type of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber reiterates the ruling that it made earlier, that evidence as to what happened at Omarska is relevant to the indictment. Continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let me raise something. Perhaps to clarify matters, could you, Mr. Mundis, see what was said during the Pre-Trial Conference so that it's clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we could have the next break to do that and report upon it immediately after the break, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Sorry to butt in. It ought to be made clear be whether my learned friend Mr. Vucicevic means the Pre-Trial Conference as held before the Trial Chamber or simply a conference held between counsel in the Prosecution's offices prior to the trial. I'm loath for the details of conferences held inter-counsel to be, as it were, discussed before the Trial Chamber. Those conversations should generally be private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Pre-Trial Conference is the relevant one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before the Trial Chamber. That's what I want to be clarified, what was said in open court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I could clarify the remarks which I was referring, they were said in the conference with three counsel present, not in the open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can it be clarified if anything was said in open court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will do that during the break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when you were in Omarska that you were forced to stay on the pista?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: A great many things were happening all day long and all night long. On one occasion when I was on pista, I saw them bringing a group of inmates. And from all the buildings, rather, those who interrogated us; guards, cooks who worked in the kitchen, they all came out to see them being beaten. I remember how a guy from Ljubija was forced to beat his head against a wall, and looking stealthily, I saw around the "white house" many dead bodies. And when they took us to the lavatory and to other places I, again, saw bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to draw your attention to the Serb festival of Petrovdan. Were you in Omarska during the time of that festival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what was happening in Omarska at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of anything happening during that festival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Gunshots, screams, wails.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything unusual the following morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A truck which took away the dead, and it was fuller than usual, fuller than on other days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many bodies you saw in the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time in Omarska when you were interrogated and, if so, can you please describe that for the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of July a guard came with a small piece of paper in his hands and it had my name on it. He took me to a room on the floor above the kitchen or, rather, in the building which housed the kitchen, and told me to go to the first room to the right. And at the very entrance into that room, I received a powerful blow in the back. I entered, and there were two soldiers there and an investigator and he told me to take a chair, and after a few formal questions, to kneel down on the floor, to take off my jacket and then two more came in. He asked me which families on my street had any weapons, and before I had time to answer, they started beating me. That question then moved on to the next one, "Tell us what you know." The beating never stopped. They mostly beat me in the -- around the kidneys and that same investigator around the heart -- in the area of heart with his heel. And at some point, because I was at a loss what to do, I told him to call my neighbour, a priest, and ask him who I was and what I was. After that, the door opened and they stopped beating me, and that instructor told them to take me to pista, and that is what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person named Islam Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once, one day, as we were lying down on the pista on our bellies, Islam Bahonjic was brought back from interrogation and allowed to fall down next to my feet, and he begged for water but I couldn't give him any, and a few minutes later he went quiet. That is, he gave no more signs of life. A man carried him, and laid him down in front of the "white house".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person named Ilijaz Dobric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. He was an engineer and worked in the mine, the same mine that I used to work in. He had a characteristic scar on his face. He came back from interrogation, and he apparently walked normally. He sat down and passed away a few minutes later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've talked about being -- lying on your belly on the pista. Can you describe what the pista was and what the conditions were while you were lying there, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pista was an area in front of the kitchen or, rather, between the kitchen and the tempering shop. And we had to lie down, now the position depended on the guard's mood; sometimes on our backs, sometimes on our bellies, sometimes we were allowed to sit. At times we even spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of material was the pista made of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asphalt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the pista covered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were flower pots around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person named Huzeir Alagic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that person in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Huzeir Alagic went missing during the search in Ljubija, and the first time I saw him again was in Keraterm, and after that, he was transferred to Omarska with us. He was strangled with a wire in front of the "white house".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him after he was strangled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he survive the strangling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who strangled him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the person who strangled him a guard or a detainee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: A guard wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person named Samir Islamovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that person in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just mentioned a while ago that on one occasion, they brought inmates in a van and that they came -- that everybody came out of the rooms upstairs and from the kitchen to watch them being beaten. One of them was Samir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, previously you testified about a detainee banging his head on the wall. Could you elaborate on that briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: His nickname was Bugarin, Balgar. He lived somewhere in Croatia. When the war broke out, he came back home. And I didn't really know him or I wasn't really much in touch with him. But that day I saw a guard standing by him and ordering him to bang his head against a wall shouting at him, "Stronger." And that is what he did, and then he fell down and Blank page inserted to insure pagination corresponds between the French and the English transcripts did not move again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you testified that you saw bodies in Omarska. Can you tell us how frequently you would see these dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often, almost daily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly the condition of the bodies that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: More often than not their heads were disfigured so that even if you knew somebody before, you could not recognise him anymore. And naturally, they were all covered in blood. Their clothes were torn and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the day that you left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Between the 5th and the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go once you left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to the camp at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go there voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day while we were in Omarska, people came to tell us that the camp was being disbanded and that we were going home. So they brought some lists of sorts and began to call out. Now, many of those on those lists had already been murdered, and many were -- and there were many in the camp who were not on the lists. So they began to separate us and group us and the group that I was assigned to was ordered to board buses. And as we were boarding them, they began to beat us, to kick us. We were not allowed to raise our heads. We had to put our heads under the seats in the bus, and then they took us in the direction of Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened when you arrived on the bus at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the way to Manjaca, the buses would stop often. Some would be taken off, beaten, and then put back on the bus. Some of them were not put back on. When we arrived in Manjaca, they switched on the heating in the buses, closed the windows, and walked around looking for some more. They spent a long time looking for Nihad Basic, Hodzic, Dedo Crnalic, and some others. Those men never returned to the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you were on the bus with the heating turned up, do you know approximately what the temperature was outside at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: August in Bosnia is hot, and that August was hot too. I couldn't tell you what the temperature was, but we were all wet. There was nothing to drink. And the dew that covered the bus inside, we were licking it, and that is how the night fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you just said that you were all wet. Why were you wet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the temperature that was inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see when you got off the bus at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the day broke, we were ordered to get off, and we passed by a group of killed men lying between the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything unusual about the body by the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a body -- or rather, I saw that a body had been stripped off and that a bottle had been pushed up the -- its colon. Rather, I could still see the end of the bottle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have one other question I failed to ask you with respect to the bus. While the bus was sitting in Manjaca with the heater on, did anyone on the bus suffer any type of conditions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zvonko Tokmadzic died on the way between Omarska and Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how he died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, approximately how long did you remain in the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there until December, 1992. I left with a second group when the camp was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you have to do anything in order to be permitted to leave Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to sign documents renouncing -- ceding all our property to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, witness, I have just a couple more questions about Keraterm. You testified about Albanians in Keraterm. Do you recall how many Albanians died in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: One while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall that person's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He arrived with me. He came from Prijedor. I think he tried to hide at this other's place who was from Ljubija, but they were both detained in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Albanian whose identity you don't know, do you know where he was employed or where he worked prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the bus terminal in Prijedor, he had his sweet shop, pastry shop called Zvjezdas. I do not know whether he owned it or was an employee there, but I often saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. The Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. It's now four minutes to 11.00. We will take the break now and resume at 25 minutes after 11.00. Witness D, during the break, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. May we start with a short period in private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to insure pagination corresponds between the French and the English transcripts

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D, it's right, isn't it, that you did your ordinary national service in the JNA for 15 months in 1983-1984?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently remain with the JNA as a member of the reserve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed it's right, isn't it, that as late as September 1991, you took part in military manoeuvres in an infantry unit as part of your reserve commitment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was August/September 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from perhaps being given more equipment than usual, is it right that everything about that particular set of manoeuvres appeared to be normal, nothing exceptional?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You could not say that. There were rumours that the unit to which I belonged was even then to be sent to the front in the neighbouring Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But apart from those rumours, it's right, isn't it, that the manoeuvres were, as you told the Office of the Prosecutor, a regular thing and there appeared nothing special about them. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequently, Witness D, in October 1991, did you hear that your reserve unit was due to be called up for service in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it at that point that you -- someone attempted to serve you with your call-up papers but you declined to take them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that stage, whatever the political dynamics of the matter were, the law was that you had to go if you were summoned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you refuse to answer the legal commitment that you were given?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me that war was absurd and fratricidal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that a significant number of people followed or did as you had done and refused to answer the call-up in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was principally the Muslim and Croatian ethnic groups who followed that course; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, some Serbs, but the majority of those who refused to answer the call-up were Muslim and Croat; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't that one of the reasons why, in effect, the JNA became an almost exclusively Serb-dominated organisation; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, this is more of politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying it was because of politics that the JNA became Serb-dominated or because Muslims and Croats simply refused to answer their commitment? Could you just clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said even before that the Serbs and Muslims and Croats who signed an oath of loyalty to the Serbs were subsequently kicked out of the police, and the same went for the Yugoslav People's Army. From there too, certain Muslims and Croats were removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May we go again into private session, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to insure pagination corresponds between the French and the English transcripts

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D, there came a time in 1992 when you were -- I'm sorry, late 1991, early 1992 when you were laid off from your place of work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on unpaid leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unpaid leave. I think that's probably the same phrase that I mean. The reason for that, Witness D, was this, was it not: The Serbs had all gone to the front, and because there was no work coming into the company, the Muslims and Croats who remained had to be, as you put it, given unpaid leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that that was one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just refresh your memory as to what you told the Office of the Prosecutor, you told them about where you had been working and that, "I had to take leave until further notice as, because of the war, there was not enough work for us." Does that refresh your memory as to the reason, the only reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is -- clearly there is -- there was a misunderstanding. It was not unpaid, it was a paid leave. And the reason given, according to me, was a regular one, because there was not enough work and it was obvious that they would send us to work. I do not believe that the reason for this was my participation in the rally or my not responding to the call-up for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D, I hadn't suggested that it was. I just wanted to clarify what you told the Office of the Prosecutor and to establish with you what the reason for you being given, as you now tell us, paid leave. All right? Did you go at all to work between December 1991 and the end of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go back to my work, but back to the workshop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D, I'd like to ask you now about the circumstances in which you became a reserve police officer. The people who approached you to join the reserve, were they Muslims or were they people of different ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person with whom I established contact for the first time on this was Rade Zekan, an active-duty police officer and an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there a second active police officer who made such an approach?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I suggested to you the name Aziz Aliskovic, would that assist you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just confirm this, that the man you've described and spoken of, Esad Islamovic, was he also an active police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just help us a little more about the difference between active and reserve police officers. Would this be correct that when you speak of an active police officer, that is you are speaking of someone who was a regular police officer before the war in the civil police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the police force of which we are talking is the ordinary conventional police force whose job is to investigate crime, organise crowds at football matches, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you accept this, Witness D, that the reserve police force was a somewhat different entity prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct that before the war, one way in which you could join the reserve police force was as an alternative to going on to the reserve of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, sorry. Instead of joining the reserve, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that you come to the end of your JNA national service at the end of your 15 months, and most people are then placed on to the JNA reserve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But some people can -- are able to opt for joining the reserve police instead of carrying out a reserve army commitment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you don't know the answer to this, tell us, but can you help us? The commitment as a reserve police officer that we have just been talking about is less than the commitment you would have as a reserve soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA reservists had to go farther away from home, whereas the reserve police officers would stay near their homes. If a JNA exercise would last for several days, the police -- reserve police officers were able to go back home every night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that your reserve commitment as a reserve on the JNA was what, a couple of weeks a year, a week a year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sometimes one day, sometimes seven days, sometimes ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know people, friends or acquaintances, who had joined the reserve police in the way that I've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would this be a fair description, that compared with the reserve commitment for the army, the reserve commitment for the reserve police was very much the easy option?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reserve police received very little, if any, training as part of their commitment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very rarely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now turn, please, to the takeover of Prijedor in April, 1992? In the commune where you were living, were you aware of the fact of that takeover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not feel that, except for a tense atmosphere, if I can call it that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of the takeover, was it your understanding, did you hear, that the Serbs were indicating at that point that they had no interest in assuming authority in your particular home area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then spent a short period as a reserve police officer, obviously, before being dismissed. Did you receive any training of any kind during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although you hadn't been on the reserve police beforehand, you were then sent effectively, at the beginning, to work without any sort of background training as to what your job should be as a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reserve police officer had occasional target practice but, apart from that, had no special role. A reserve police officer would always be accompanied by an active-duty police officer when going on patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so would this be correct, that you would depend on the active police officer firstly to command you and control his unit, and secondly to tell you where to go and what to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would this be correct, that no reserve police officer within your knowledge was given promotion to a senior rank or command-and-control functions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Deputy Commander of the police station was a reserve police officer, and how he arrived at that position, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you just give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall that person's name, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Komosar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that his first name or his family name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you recall what his ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move now, please, briefly to the time when the village of Hambarine was being shelled. After that shelling, is it right that you were called to go to the police station at Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not after the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time when you were at the police station in Ljubija around the time of the shelling, and you were there with other police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first shelling started a day before the second shelling. During -- it was during the second shelling that we were called up to the police station, and I went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it on that occasion that you were informed that -- of the likelihood of the Serbs taking over the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that you should stay on with a view to controlling Serb extremists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just remind you again of what you told the Office of the Prosecutor? "At the station, we were told by the Deputy Commander Komosar, the commander being trapped in Prijedor at that moment and unable to return, that the Serbs were taking over, but that we should stay on to control the Serb extremists." Do you remember saying that to the Office of the Prosecutor? Blank page inserted to insure pagination corresponds between the French and the English transcripts

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not us but he.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, unless it's been mistranslated, the version that we have says, "We should stay on to control the Serb extremists." Are you now saying that that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: Komosar told us, after a brief break when he cried, that he would try to stay and prevent the Serb extremists from entering the police station. That is, that he would allow some honest Serbs and prevent Serb extremists from becoming Serb police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand by the phrase "Serb extremists" to mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Former criminals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Criminals in the sense of people who had committed crimes like theft or robbery or things like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D, doesn't the word -- the phrase "Serb extremists" mean precisely what it meant when used of Muslim extremists when used by Serbs, people involved in politics or the military? Isn't that what it meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: An extremist or criminal of any ethnic background is the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just returning briefly to the officer Aziz Aliskovic, did you hear of him being part of a detachment in control of a checkpoint at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if that officer was in control of that checkpoint when the incident involving the death of some Serbs took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what you heard. Did you, amongst the things you heard, hear of him being in charge when that checkpoint -- there was an incident at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly, but I think that the zone of responsibility of the Ljubija station extended to Tukovi. And I believe, but I do not affirm, that Aziz was on regular duty at the checkpoint at Hambarine just as the rest of us were assigned to other checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put a date on the incident when some Serbs had been approaching in a vehicle and managed to get themselves killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even approximately. Was it early May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe even later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D, as to your fellow officers who served with you as reserve police officers, how many were there who were working with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know exactly. Some were on duty which means that they were -- would not come to the station, they were on duty in Surkovac so I would not be able to tell you the exact number. We were never able to all gather at the station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Are you able to give us an approximate figure for how many were involved, Witness D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to 50, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of those officers, were they exclusively Muslim or were they of mixed ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of mixed ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can move on now, please, to your first -- the first occasion when you were detained, which I think was about 10 days after you were dismissed from the reserve police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was on that same day, was it not, that you became aware of Serbs in military uniform close to your own home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before my arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those soldiers it was, I think, who gave you advice, if I can call it that, about your -- the women of the area taking off valuables to prevent looters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are not quite right, sir. I mentioned -- I said that it happened at the time when Ljubija was searched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it perhaps matters not when it took place. It's just simply I want to establish that some Serb soldiers gave you that advice at some stage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is right, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those same soldiers indicated to you that they would put on a show of searching your house but wouldn't damage or steal anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they keep to their word concerning that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning now to the second occasion when you were arrested --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I was still not arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can we come to the 18th or 19th of June. At that stage you were detained; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was in the early hours of the 19th of June that some men came to fetch you and you were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was later. It was about 7.00 or 8.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in any event, you were taken to the police station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst those who were detained at the same time, were there two Albanians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
